s: alternative spelling of heofonum: dative plural of heofon
third-person singular present indicative of hēofan
Eall þā lēaf sind brūn, and sē heofon grǣġ.
All the leaves are brown, and the sky is gray.

late 9th century, King Alfred's translation of Boethius' The Consolation of Philosophy
Sē heofon bringþ lēohte dagas and eft behileþ þæt lēoht mid þīestrum.
The sky brings bright days and then hides the light with darkness.

late 10th century, Ælfric, Lives of Saints
Æfter þisum ġebede, bærst ūt of heofonum swȳþe fǣrlīċ fȳr and forbernde þæt templ, and ealle þā godas grundlunga suncon intō þǣre eorþan, and ne ætēowdon siþþan.
After this prayer, a very sudden fire burst out of the heavens and burned up the temple, and all the gods sunk completely into the earth, and have not appeared since.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hebn. Probably related to both Proto-West Germanic *himil and Proto-Germanic *himinaz, but the origins of the relationship are mysterious.
From heofon (“heaven”) + -cund (“coming from, -like”). Cognate with Gothic himinakunds.

s: the king of heaven, heavenly king.
y: From heofon (“heaven”) + cyning (“king”). Cognate with Old Saxon himilkuning, Old High German himilkuning.
From heofon (“sky”) + fȳr (“fire”). Means "fire from the sky".
From heofon + -isċ. Compare with Old Saxon himilisk, Old High German himilisk, Old Frisian himelesk, Old Norse hifneskr, himneskr.

s: A title for God; Heavenly Father

y: Equivalent to heofon + rīċe, possibly as a calque of Latin regnum caelōrum. Cognate with Old Saxon hevanrīki, Old High German himilrīhhi (German Himmelreich), Old Norse himinnrīki (Danish himmerige).

s: Seo mænigeo mære wære swa heofonsteorran.
The multitude should be as great as the stars of heaven.
The stars of heaven shall fall.

y: From heofon (“heaven”) + tungol (“star, planet”). Cognate with Old Saxon himiltungal, Old High German himilzungal, Icelandic himintungl.
From heofon (“heaven”) + weard (“guard”). Cognate with Old Saxon hevanwarda (“angel”).

s: a cloud in the sky, cloud of heaven
y: From heofon + wolcen. Compare Old Saxon himilwolcan, Old High German himilwolchen.

s: the glory of heaven; heavenly glory

y: From a metathesis of Proto-West Germanic *hehlā, from Proto-Germanic *hehlǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel(h₂)- (“to freeze; cold”). Cognate with Old Norse héla.
From Proto-West Germanic *heluru, from Proto-Germanic *helurō (“balance, scales”), from Proto-Indo-European *kel- (“to protrude; high”).

s: to weigh in the balance, ponder

y: From heolstor (“darkness, place of concealment”) + loca (“enclosure”).

s:
Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
Sēo tīd onginð on ðisum Sunnandæġe, nigon wucon ǣr Ēastron, and ġeendað on ðām Saternesdæġe þǣre Ēasterlīċan wucan: tō ðām dæġe sind heonon ġetealde hundseofontiġ daga; and þæt Israhela folc, for heora māndǣdum and forgǣġednyssum, wurdon ġehergode, and hundseofontiġ ġēara on Babilonisċum þēowdōme, buton blisse and myrhðe, wunodon.

This time begins this Sunday, nine weeks before Easter, and ends on the Saturday in the week of Easter: to that day, from today, are seventy days; and the Israelites, for their evil deeds and transgressions, were taken captive, and spent seventy years living in slavery to the Bablyonians, without joy or mirth.
y: From a variant of the Germanic root of hē. Cognate with Old Saxon hinana, Old High German hinana (German hinnen).

s: from now on, beyond this point

Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
Đā ġelǣredan ne beðurfon þyssera bōca, forðan ðe him mæġ heora āgen lār genihtsumian. Iċ cweðe nū þæt iċ næfre heonon forð ne āwende gōdspel oððe gōdspeltrahtas of Ledene on Englisċ.
The learned have no need of these books, for they can be satisfied by their own learning. I say now that henceforth, I will never translate a gospel or a gospel-commentary from Latin into English.
genitive of hīe: their, of them

y: From Proto-West Germanic *hauʀukōn, *hauʀikōn, equivalent to hīeran + -cian.
From Proto-Germanic *herdō, from Proto-Indo-European *kerdʰ- (“file, row, herd”). Compare Old Saxon herda, Old High German herta, Old Norse hjǫrð, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌰 (hairda).
From Proto-Germanic *heuraz, *hiurijaz. Compare Old Armenian սէր (sēr, “love”).

s: Heorot, the mead hall of Hrothgar in Beowulf

y: From Proto-West Germanic *herut, from Proto-Germanic *herutaz, from Proto-Indo-European *kerud- (Ancient Greek κόρυδος (kórudos, “crested lark”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱerh₂- (Latin cervus (“horn”)). Germanic cognates include Old Saxon hirot, Old High German hiruz, and Old Norse hjǫrtr.
From Proto-West Germanic *herʀō or *her(r)ō, from Proto-Germanic *herzô or *her(r)ô.
From Proto-West Germanic *herʀā or *her(r)ā, from Proto-Germanic *herzǫ or *her(r)ǫ.

s:
c. 992, Ælfric, "Sermon on the Nativiity of Our Lord"
Ðyllīce word María hēold ārǣfniġende on hire heortan.
Such words Mary held, pondering them in her heart.

Homilies of the Anglo-Saxon Church
Woruldcara, and welan, and flǣsċlīċe lustas forsmoriað ðǣs mōdes ðrotan, and ne geðafiað gōdne willan infaran tō his heortan, swilċe hī ðone līflīċan blǣd forðrǣstne ācwellon. Twā wiðerrǣde ðing geðēodde Drihten on ðisum cwyde, þæt sind ymhīdiġnyssa and lustas.

Concern about worldly things, and wealth, and carnal lusts choke the throat of the mind, and do not allow good will into the heart, as if they killed it by crushing the living fruit. The Lord connected two contrary things in this saying, which are cares and lusts.
y:
From Proto-West Germanic *hertā.
Cognate with Old Frisian herte, Old Saxon herta, Old Dutch herta, Old High German herza, Old Norse hjarta, Gothic 𐌷𐌰𐌹𐍂𐍄𐍉 (hairtō). The Indo-European root is also the source of Greek καρδία (kardía), Latin cor, Welsh craidd, Russian се́рдце (sérdce), Lithuanian širdis.
From Proto-West Germanic *heru, from Proto-Germanic *heruz. Cognate with Old Norse hjǫrr (“sword”).
From Proto-Germanic *Herugaizaz, equivalent to heoru (“sword”) + gār (“spear”).
Unclear. Possibly related to hēah (“high”), or perhaps related to Ancient Greek κῠ́τος (kŭ́tos, “hollow”), also of unclear origin.

s: late 10th century, Ælfric, the Old English Hexateuch, Genesis 46:2
God heard him and called out, "Jacob, Jacob!" And he answered him and said, "Here I am!"
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hēr, from Proto-Germanic *hē₂r, apparently from the stem *hi- (“this”); the exact formation is unclear. Cognate with Old Saxon hēr, Old High German hiar, Old Norse hér, Gothic 𐌷𐌴𐍂 (hēr).

s: follower, servant, one who obeys another

late 9th century, translation of Bede's Ecclesiastical History
In þǣre þēode was in þā tīd Sǣberht cyning, Æðelberhtes swustorsunu ⁊ his hēra.
At that time Seaberht was king of that province; he was the nephew and follower of Athelberht.

Hwīlum iċ on wloncum wiċġe rīde herġes on ende; heard is mīn tunge.
Sometimes, I ride on a proud horse at the rear of an army; my tongue in hard.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *hari, from Proto-Germanic *harjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ker-.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *Harjabalþ, from *hari (“army”) + *balþ (“bold, brave”). Equivalent to here + beald. Cognate with Old High German Heribald.
From Proto-West Germanic *harjabergōn. By surface analysis, herebeorg + -ian.

From Proto-West Germanic *Harjaburg, from Proto-Germanic *Harjaburgz, from *harjaz (“army”) + *burgz (“fortification”). Equivalent to here + burg. Cognate with Old High German Heriburg, Old Norse Herborg.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
An. DCCCXXXIII Hēr ġefeaht Eċġbriht cing wið XXXV sċiphlæsta æt Carrum ⁊ þǣr wearð myċel wæl ġesleġen, ⁊ þā Denisċan ahton wælstōwe ġeweald. ⁊ Hereferð ⁊ Wiġþeġn, tweġen bisċeopas, forðferdan, ⁊ Duda ⁊ Ōsmōd, tweġen ealdormenn, forðferdon.

Year 833 In this year King Edgebright fought against thirty-five shiploads of men at Charmouth, and many were slain, and the Danes took control of the battlefield. And two bishops, Herefrith and Wigthegn, and two aldermen, Duda and Osmod, died.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *Harjafriþu, from *hari (“army”) + *friþu (“peace”). Equivalent to here + friþ. Cognate with Old High German Herifrid.

s: [H]eregeatu means literally ‘war-gear’ but it had a technical sense referring to the dues, originally consisting of war equipment, to be repaid to a lord on his tenant’s death.

y: From Proto-West Germanic *Harjagern, from *hari (“army”) + *gern (“eager, willing”). Equivalent to here + ġeorn. Cognate with Old High German Herigern.
From Proto-West Germanic *Harjagunþi, from *hari (“army”) + *gunþi (“battle”). Equivalent to here + gūþ. Cognate with Old High German Herigund.

s:
The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
Þȳ ilcan ġēare forbarn Lundenbyriġ, ⁊ on þām ilcan ġēare forðferdon tweġen ealdormenn, Æþelmǣr on Hāmtūnsċīre ⁊ Ēadwine on Sūþseaxum. ⁊ Æþelmǣres līc līð on Wintanċeastre on nīwan mynstre, ⁊ Ēadwines on þām mynstre æt Abbandūne. Þǣs ilcan ġēare forðferdon twā abbodessan on Dorsǣtum, Herelufu on Sċeaftesbyriġ ⁊ Wulfwin on Werhām.

In the same year [982], London burned down, and in the same year, two princes passed away: Ethelmer in Hamptonshire and Edwin in Sussex. Ethemer's body lies in the new monastery in Winchester, and Edwin's in the monastery at Abingdon. In the same year, two abbesses passed away in Dorset: Herelufu in Shaftesbury and Wulfwin in Wareham.
y: From Proto-West Germanic *Harjalubu, from *hari (“army”) + *lubu (“love”). Equivalent to here + lufu. Cognate with Old High German Heriluba.
From Proto-Germanic *harjamann-. Equivalent to here (“army”) + mann (“man”).
From Proto-West Germanic *Harjamōd, from Proto-Germanic *Harjamōdaz. Equivalent to here (“army”) + mōd (“spirt, courage”).
